#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug



#### What this PR does / why we need it:

This PR fixes a bug where after a custom resource version is no longer served an owned resource created at this version is not garbage collected. We now update API versions of owned resources in GC's
in-memory dependency graph.

#### Which issue(s) this PR fixes: 
<!--
*Automatically closes linked issue when PR is merged.
Usage: `Fixes #<issue number>`, or `Fixes (paste link of issue)`.
_If PR is about `failing-tests or flakes`, please post the related issues/tests in a comment and do not use `Fixes`_*
-->
Fixes #102641 

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

I have manually tested that with this the resources now get garbage collected correctly in the scenario described in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/102641#issuecomment-857809490 .

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?
<!--
If no, just write "NONE" in the release-note block below.
If yes, a release note is required:

For more information on release notes see: https://git.k8s.io/community/contributors/guide/release-notes.md
-->
```release-note
Fixes a bug where owned CRs were not garbage collected after a CR version removal.
```

issue_context.title: owned Custom Resources not garbage collected after CRD API version removal
issue_context.body:
<!-- Please use this template while reporting a bug and provide as much info as possible. Not doing so may result in your bug not being addressed in a timely manner. Thanks!

If the matter is security related, please disclose it privately via https://kubernetes.io/security/
-->


#### What happened:

We are trying to deprecate and remove some CRD API versions and as part of that to ensure that users who have originally deployed Custom Resources at the legacy versions can upgrade.
For a Custom Resource X that is a dependent on another Custom Resource Y and they both have been originally created using a legacy API version `v1alpha2`, we observe that after an upgrade to a controller version where `v1alpha2` is no longer served, X is not garbage collected after Y has been deleted.

X after the upgrade:
```
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: CertificateRequest
metadata:
  annotations:
    cert-manager.io/certificate-name: test1
...
name: test1-4d8sc
  namespace: default
  ownerReferences:
  - apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1alpha2
    blockOwnerDeletion: true
    controller: true
    kind: Certificate
    name: test1
    uid: a20001e7-4793-42bf-955a-a6216cbdc933
...
```

Y after the upgrade:
```
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: Certificate
metadata:
...
  name: test1
  namespace: default
  resourceVersion: "12276"
  uid: a20001e7-4793-42bf-955a-a6216cbdc933
```

In the above config `CertificateRequest.metadata.ownerReferences[0].apiVersion` is incorrect. I thought that perhaps this is the issue, so I tried editing it `v1alpha2` -> `v1` just before running the delete command. The edited `CertificateRequest` was still not deleted.
Does the `metadata.ownerReferences[0].apiVersion` matter- I seem to remember seeing somewhere on #sig-api-machinery Slack that it is not actually used?

#### What you expected to happen:

I expected that X would be deleted after Y is deleted as it happens normally with these resources.

#### How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible):
1. Deploy `cert-manager` version `v0.16` where the storage version for all CRDs is `v1alpha2`
2. Create an `Certificate` (Y) Custom Resource using the `v1alpha2` API. A `CertificateRequest` X will be created for Y with Y set as X's owner reference.
3. Upgrade to a newer version of `cert-manager` where the only storage version is `v1` (`v1alpha2` is still being served)
4. Upgrade stored versions of Custom Resources and `status.storedVersions` of CRDs as described in Kubernetes docs [here](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/extend-kubernetes/custom-resources/custom-resource-definition-versioning/#upgrade-existing-objects-to-a-new-stored-version)
5. Upgrade to a version of `cert-manager` where `v1` is the only served version
6. Delete Y `kubectl delete certificate test1`
7. Observe that X is not deleted even after ~30 minutes, and `deletionTimestamp` is not set. 

#### Anything else we need to know?:

Please let me know how I can go about debugging this or any additional information I could provide?

#### Environment:
- Kubernetes version (use `kubectl version`):
on GKE:
```
Client Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"20", GitVersion:"v1.20.2", GitCommit:"faecb196815e248d3ecfb03c680a4507229c2a56", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2021-01-13T13:28:09Z", GoVersion:"go1.15.5", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"}
Server Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"20+", GitVersion:"v1.20.6-gke.1000", GitCommit:"3ae0998c5052f420a17cb96bacf860ec5d6822a3", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2021-04-29T09:17:16Z", GoVersion:"go1.15.10b5", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"}
```
on Kind:
```
Client Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"20", GitVersion:"v1.20.2", GitCommit:"faecb196815e248d3ecfb03c680a4507229c2a56", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2021-01-13T13:28:09Z", GoVersion:"go1.15.5", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"}
Server Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"21", GitVersion:"v1.21.1", GitCommit:"5e58841cce77d4bc13713ad2b91fa0d961e69192", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2021-05-18T01:10:20Z", GoVersion:"go1.16.4", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"}
```

- OS (e.g: `cat /etc/os-release`):
- Kernel (e.g. `uname -a`): `Linux irbe-XPS-13-9310 5.8.0-53-generic #60-Ubuntu SMP Thu May 6 07:46:32 UTC 2021 x86_64 x86_64 x86_64 GNU/Linux`
- Install tools: kubectl, helm
- Network plugin and version (if this is a network-related bug):
- Others:

/cc @munnerz

The apiversion is used in gc [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d849d9d057369121fc43aa3359059471e1ca9d1c/pkg/controller/garbagecollector/operations.go#L64).

Since v1apha1 did not exist anymore, that should trigger this error [message](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d849d9d057369121fc43aa3359059471e1ca9d1c/pkg/controller/garbagecollector/garbagecollector.go#L348). If you ran the apiserver with `-v=5`, I would expect this error message in the controller manager log. If that's the case, then it explained why X was not deleted.

But you said that even if you manually fixed the ownerReference before deleting Y, X still wouldn't get gc'ed. I don't know why that's the case. Did you wait for some time between fixing the ownerRef and deleting Y? Did X always not get gc'ed or was the behavior flaky?

cc @liggitt who might know similar issues.

Hi @caesarxuchao ,

Thank you for the reply.

I tried to increase the log level as you suggested. From the errors I saw, it appears that somehow the garbage collector has the wrong API version for the _owned_ resource. I've copied the steps from the issue description with where the errors appear:

Steps followed (here `CertificateRequest` X is the owned resource and `Certificate` Y is the owner resource):
1. Deploy cert-manager version `v0.16` where the storage version for all CRDs is `v1alpha2`,
2. Create a `Certificate` (Y) Custom Resource using the `v1alpha2` API. A CertificateRequest X will be created for Y with Y set as X's owner reference.
3. Upgrade to a newer version of cert-manager where the only storage version is `v1` (`v1alpha2` is still being served, so is `v1beta1`)
4. Upgrade stored versions of Custom Resources and `status.storedVersions` of CRDs as described in Kubernetes docs. Also manually edit `metadata.ownerReferences[x].apiVersion for X. Wait for about ~10 minutes
5. Upgrade to a version of cert-manager where `v1` is the only served version
6. Observe some errors in controller manager's logs:

```
I0609 15:15:42.220403       1 graph_builder.go:632] GraphBuilder process object: v1/ConfigMap, namespace kube-system, name cert-manager-cainjector-leader-election, uid 074426be-cef1-40e3-ad04-5fc09b9d092c, event type update, virtual=false
```
At this point the `v1beta1`, `v1alpha2` APIs are no longer served. In step 4 I had ran `kubectl get certificaterequest test2-tx5zn -oyaml | kubectl apply -f -` to enforce update of the stored version in etcd and checked that the `kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration` annotation now shows the `v1` API version. I assumed that since I can still view and retrieve the `CertificateRequest` after the alpha and beta APIs are no longer served the stored version got updated correctly? I also tried deleting the `kube-controller-manager-kind-control-plane` pod (on `kind`) in case the old version was somehow cashed by the garbage controller- but still saw the same errors.

> I wonder why we haven't seen similar GC issues when Kubernetes stopped serving apps/v1beta1 and apiextensions/v1beta1 in the past releases. @liggitt do you know?

likely because that was paired with a Kubernetes upgrade which eventually restarted the kube-controller-manager, at which point it picked up the apps/v1 versions of those resources

@caesarxuchao sorry for the delay!

> Perhaps we can fix the issue here, here GC observes an object is updated, we can let GC checks if the APIVersion in the update event is the same as the APIVersion recorded in the in-memory node, if not, updates the in-memory APIVersion. @irbekrm do you have time to write&test a patch?

[Updating the API version when the object is updated](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/103033/commits/1ada461ee968a8f07512cd45be9cd462b66a3806) seems to fix it. I built this version a couple of times with the scenario described in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/102641#issuecomment-857809490 and saw the owned resource being correctly garbage collected each time.

> Somehow the Owner's APIVersion is updated (APIVersion:"cert-manager.io/v1", Kind:"Certificate"). I actually don't know why the APIVersion of the owner is up-to-date.

It seemed to get updated [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/garbagecollector/graph_builder.go#L685) at least in the scenarios I tested.

I submitted a tentative PR with a one-line fix for this, but have not yet looked at updating the tests to test this change.

> It seemed to get updated here at least in the scenarios I tested.

I see. The ownerRef was updated to the new version. But perhaps the in-memory node that represented the owner object still had the old version.

I noticed a different but highly related issue. The story is like this:

We have a CRD called `DeploymentWorkload` (DW) with an operator that generates a corresponding [FederatedDeployment](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/kubefed) (FDP) for each DW. The FDP should be deleted when the corresponding DW is deleted, so we set an `ownerReference` in FDP that references the DW.

The problem comes when the federation manager synchronizes the FDP (which has an existent DW) on a fedhost cluster to a deployment on the fedmember cluster, which copies over the `ownerReferences` in the FDP [^1], i.e. we end up creating Deployment objects with an ownerReference on a nonexistent DW. Since DW is a CRD that is only intended to be used in the fedhost cluster, it is not applied on the fedmember cluster, so the deployment is working correctly so far, and nobody noticed that something is wrong because nothing works incorrectly and no controller emits logs anywhere. Until one day, an operator, for whatever reason, *creates* the DW CRD on the fedmember cluster, then all deployment objects start getting deleted because the API version now exists [^3]. Then you look at the controller logs and notice no abnormal behavior, see that controller manager is deleting these objects, and figure out that the garbage collector controller is causing issues, and realize that there's an invalid ownerReference, and still have no idea how come this never caused a problem before, because typically, one would never expect that **creating a CRD would delete a bunch of deployments even in a basic Kubernetes setup with no custom controllers** [^2].

We can avoid this problem in the future by creating a webhook that blocks the creation of ownerReferences (in CREATE and UPDATE events) referencing nonexistent resource types (no matter the object exists or not) for all objects, or alternatively, create a controller that raises alerts for such events. But I think this sounds like a potential risk to Kubernetes users in general, and this should probably be improved.

A possible non-intrusive mitigation (before deciding on either of the two more dangerous solutions described in the code comments) is to simply generate a WARN-level log message here, before assuming that the object should not be deleted:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/b74d023e70d6064c7f3f77031e7d26ec38497fc9/pkg/controller/garbagecollector/garbagecollector.go#L408-L417

[^1]: We are using an internal modified version of kubefed, so I am not sure if the public version of kubefed also has this behaviour. I know this particular incident is most likely an issue with our kubefed setup that `ownerReferences` should be copied over.
[^2]: This is a worst case speculation. Fortunately we created the CRD in a test cluster before it caused online damage.
[^3]: To be exact, the garbage collector does not immediately delete the deployments since the controller does not handle CRD creation directly. I am not sure what causes the actual deletion after CRD creation a few minutes later; perhaps pod updates reflected to the deployment status?

Hi. I stumbled onto this thread when trying to understand whether the mentioned behavior is the default behavior of the garbage collector. 

i.e., by default, does the garbage collector watch resources of every CRD?
In the example in this issue, can X and Y, be resources with any custom group, version and kind? 
Can X and Y have a different version? And a different group? 
Should I expect the garbage collector to delete X after Y is deleted, by default? 

_hopefully, someone's still following this thread. :)_

> But I think this sounds like a potential risk to Kubernetes users in general, and this should probably be improved.

Deleting objects whose referenced owners can be verified to be absent is sort of the whole job of GC, so the scenario you are describing is working as intended. Being resilient to an unresolveable owner type for a long time is necessary in a distributed system where the backing server for an owner type might be unavailable for long stretches of time.

> A possible non-intrusive mitigation (before deciding on either of the two more dangerous solutions described in the code comments) is to simply generate a WARN-level log message here, before assuming that the object should not be deleted

I think this is already logged, but at a very low verbosity. Because this scenario could persist for a long time, and unresolveable owner references are regularly re-checked, raising the verbosity here risks flooding logs in steady state.

> by default, does the garbage collector watch resources of every CRD?

Yes

> In the example in this issue, can X and Y, be resources with any custom group, version and kind?

Yes

> Can X and Y have a different version? And a different group?

Yes

> Should I expect the garbage collector to delete X after Y is deleted, by default?

Yes, for any given instance of custom resource X and custom resource Y. When individual instances are removed, GC is working properly. When instance `my-x` of type X has an owner `my-y` of type Y, and the entire type Y is removed, there's a race between:
1. GC observing the removal of the `my-y` instance and verifying it is gone while the endpoints of type Y are still being served
2. The endpoints for type Y being removed, and GC falling back to treating `my-x` as having an owner reference with an unresolveable type (and waiting for endpoints for type Y to exist so it can verify instance `my-y` is absent)

> Being resilient to an unresolveable owner type for a long time is necessary in a distributed system where the backing server for an owner type might be unavailable for long stretches of time.

The problem is, it is not a problem with the inevitable problems like network errors in a distributed system, but with misconfiguration that should require immediate user intervention. And while garbage collection is meant to delete objects, in general one wouldn't expect it to delete a lot of objects in a short period of time, particularly objects that were created months ago (instead of objects created during GC downtime).

A few observations:

1. This code is only run in the case where the add/update modifies ownerReferences of the observed object (it runs in the `if len(added) != 0 || len(removed) != 0 || len(changed) != 0 {` block)... it won't run if the only thing changing is the apiVersion/kind of the observed object

2. `identity` isn't safe to update, since other threads read from this field and assume it is immutable... we would have to do something like what is done above when transitioning from an unobserved node to an observed node:

    ```
    existingNode = existingNode.clone()
    existingNode.identity.APIVersion = event.gvk.GroupVersion().String()
    existingNode.identity.Kind = event.gvk.Kind
    gb.uidToNode.Write(existingNode)
    ```

3. We should only do this swap when the observed apiVersion/kind doesn't match the existing identity, and the event we're observing is not a virtual event

4. This deserves testcases added to TestConflictingData
